resources.title: Finding Color in the City
resources.excerpt: A practical way to notice, frame, and layer color while photographing everyday city life.
resources.imageAlt: Bright color and geometry in a Los Angeles street scene
resources.imageCaption: Los Angeles — color becomes the subject when you give it room to lead.
introduction: Color is often the first thing that stops me on a walk. It can turn an ordinary corner into a photograph, create a visual rhythm, or connect people to the space around them.
The goal is not to chase every bright surface. It is to recognize when color is doing meaningful work inside the frame.

sections.heading: Start with one anchor color
paragraphs: Choose one color in the scene and let it organize the frame. A painted wall, a jacket, or a small sign can give your eye a place to land.
points: Look for repetition across the foreground and background.
Move until distracting colors fall outside the frame.
Wait for a person or gesture to complete the composition.

sections.heading: Use light to simplify
paragraphs: Strong light separates colors and creates useful blocks of shadow. Overcast light is quieter, but it can reveal subtler combinations and hold detail across the whole scene.

takeaways: Check every edge of the frame.
Let the moment come to your composition.

resources.title: Build a Better Photo Walk
resources.excerpt: A simple, repeatable practice for staying observant and returning home with more intentional frames.
resources.imageAlt: A candid urban photograph made during a photo walk
resources.imageCaption: A good walk is measured in attention, not distance.
introduction: A photo walk works best when it has enough structure to focus your attention and enough freedom to follow surprise.

sections.heading: Set one constraint
paragraphs: Before leaving, choose a small assignment: photograph only at intersections, follow one color, use one focal length, or stay within six blocks.
points: Walk the same route more than once.
Review for patterns, not just favorites.

sections.heading: Slow down before moving on
paragraphs: When a background has potential, stay with it. Make a clean frame first, then wait to see what people, light, or motion add to it.

takeaways: Edit after some distance from the shoot.

resources.title: Editing a Cohesive Photo Series
resources.excerpt: Move beyond selecting single favorites and shape a group of photographs with rhythm, contrast, and purpose.
resources.imageAlt: A colorful photograph selected for a cohesive series
resources.imageCaption: A series creates meaning between photographs, not only within them.
introduction: Editing a series asks a different question than choosing your best individual photographs. The strongest image is not always the one the sequence needs.

sections.heading: Make a generous first edit
paragraphs: Pull every photograph that speaks to the idea, feeling, place, or visual language of the project. Then look for recurring gestures and relationships.
points: Print small thumbnails or use a broad grid view.
Remove duplicate ideas before weaker photographs.
Notice how your eye moves from frame to frame.

sections.heading: Build rhythm with contrast
paragraphs: Alternate dense and quiet compositions, wide scenes and details, or stillness and motion. Variety gives each image space while a consistent visual language holds the work together.

takeaways: Edit for the whole, not the hero image.
End before the idea feels exhausted.
